name: Oral cyproterone acetate
lead: Cyproterone acetate (CPA) is a steroidal antiandrogen and progestin sold alone as Androcur and, combined with ethinylestradiol, as Diane-35, Dianette and similar products.[1] For hair, it is used in some countries as an off-label or labelled treatment for scalp hair loss, hirsutism, acne and seborrhea in women with androgen-related signs.[1][2]

People seek it for clearer skin, less oily skin and reduced unwanted facial and body hair, and for slowing androgen-driven thinning of scalp hair, because it lowers androgen signalling in the skin and hair follicle.[1] It is also used in feminizing hormone therapy, where its antiandrogen and antigonadotropin actions reduce testosterone and support feminine body changes.[1]

It was first synthesised at Schering in 1961 and reached the market as an antiandrogen in Europe in 1973; it has never been marketed in the United States.[1] Documented risks include liver toxicity, blood clots and meningioma, and the European Medicines Agency issued a warning in 2020 about meningioma at higher doses.[1] Because of its effects on male hormones, use for hair loss in men is described as generally impractical.[1]
infobox: Prescription only; not marketed in the US

paras: Wikipedia lists acne, hirsutism, seborrhea, scalp hair loss and hidradenitis suppurativa in women among its uses, usually as a low-dose combined pill with ethinylestradiol.[1] It reports that a low-dose pill improved acne in 75 to 90 percent of women and that up to 70 percent relapsed after stopping.[1]

A registered European survey (NCT04925180) of physician awareness of Androcur and cyproterone safety information names androgenisation signs in women, including hirsutism, androgenetic alopecia, acne and seborrhea, among the treatment contexts.[3]

For hirsutism, Wikipedia reports cyproterone acetate given cyclically with an estrogen, with efficacy described as similar to spironolactone, flutamide and finasteride; adding extra cyproterone to a standard pill containing 2 mg was reported as no more effective, or only marginally more effective, than the pill alone for severe hirsutism.[1] High-dose use alone is also reported to have improved acne in 75 to 90 percent of women.[1] In men, studies are reported to show improved acne and halted progression of scalp hair loss, but demasculinization, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, bone density loss and reversible infertility make use impractical in most cases.[1]

The drug is also used for polycystic ovary syndrome and other androgen excess states, in feminizing hormone therapy (WPATH SOC8 recommends no more than 10 mg a day), and at high doses for prostate cancer and to reduce sex drive in paraphilias.[1]

In transgender women, use was first reported in 1977 and was well established by the early 1990s. Studies reported full testosterone suppression with estrogen across a range of oral doses, and Wikipedia notes that, unlike spironolactone with estrogen, cyproterone acetate with estrogen consistently brings testosterone into the female range. Spironolactone is more common in the US, while cyproterone acetate is widely used in Europe and elsewhere.[1] Breast growth is often a desired outcome in this context.[1] A combined product with estradiol valerate is used for menopausal symptoms in more than 40 countries.[1]

CPA blocks the androgen receptor, is a progestogen that suppresses gonadotropins, and has weak glucocorticoid activity but no estrogenic activity; oral bioavailability is 68 to 100 percent and it is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4.[1] Its progestin pharmacology is reviewed in a 2003 Maturitas classification of progestins.[4]
Grokipedia's page concerns the related parent compound cyproterone, not the acetate; it describes CPA as the ester that gained progestogenic and antigonadotropic activity.[5]

Wikipedia describes it as a highly potent progestogen, a moderately potent antiandrogen and a weak partial glucocorticoid, with no estrogenic or antimineralocorticoid activity. Its antigonadotropic action suppresses sex hormones in both sexes.[1] It is about 93 percent albumin-bound; oral half-life is reported as roughly 1.6 to 4.3 days, and about 70 percent is excreted in feces and 30 percent in urine. A major metabolite is 15beta-hydroxycyproterone acetate.[1] Chemically it is a pregnane steroid, the acetylated derivative of 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone, related to chlormadinone acetate and medroxyprogesterone acetate.[1]

Wikipedia lists gynecomastia, reduced libido and erectile dysfunction in men, fatigue, depression and weight gain at high doses, and rarer liver toxicity (including failure and tumors), raised prolactin, blood clots and meningioma.[1] Abrupt discontinuation of high doses can cause adrenal insufficiency, and pregnancy, liver disease, prior thromboembolism and meningioma are contraindications.[1]

The EMA warned in 2020 that doses of 25 mg a day or more may increase meningioma risk and recommended alternatives where possible, except for prostate cancer.[1] Two 2009 BMJ studies of hormonal contraception and venous thromboembolism compared risk by progestogen type and oestrogen dose, and reported higher risk with pills containing cyproterone acetate than with some other progestogens.[6][7]

Reported frequencies include very common headache, tiredness, reduced libido, reduced ejaculate volume, inhibited spermatogenesis in men, inhibited ovulation in women, and raised liver enzymes; common effects include weight change, depressed mood, gynecomastia, breast pain, irregular menstruation and hot flashes.[1] Rare liver toxicity includes jaundice, hepatitis and liver failure, and benign and malignant liver tumors are reported as very rare.[1] Drug interactions include CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole and itraconazole and inducers such as rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine and St. John's wort, which can lower cyproterone levels substantially.[1] Wikipedia notes no deaths have been associated with overdose.[1]

Registered studies include trials of cyproterone-containing pills in polycystic ovary syndrome, hyperandrogenism and menstrual disorders, and a bioequivalence study.[8][9][10] No placebo-controlled trial of oral cyproterone acetate for androgenetic alopecia is cited here; effectiveness for scalp hair is described mainly in reviews and clinical practice.

Wikipedia's account of dermatologic studies is drawn from clinical series: low-dose pills with ethinylestradiol improved acne in roughly 75 to 90 percent of women, and relapse after stopping occurred in up to 70 percent.[1] WPATH Standards of Care version 8 recommends a maximum oral daily dose of 10 mg in feminizing therapy, citing risks such as fatigue, clots, benign brain tumors and liver damage.[1]

CPA was synthesised in 1961 by Rudolf Wiechert at Schering, originally as a progestin intended for threatened abortion; a patent naming Friedmund Neumann followed in 1962.[1] Its antiandrogenic activity was discovered serendipitously in 1963 and reported in rats by Neumann in 1965; first clinical use came in 1966 for sexual deviance and prostate cancer, and it was first studied for androgen-dependent skin and hair conditions in 1969.[1] Androcur was approved in Europe in 1973, the first antiandrogen introduced for medical use; an injectable form followed in 1977 and the Diane pill with ethinylestradiol in 1978. Canada followed in 1987 and Diane-35 in 1998.[1]

Wikipedia reports that it was never marketed in the US, reportedly due to concerns about breast tumors in beagles and teratogenicity; US clinicians use alternatives such as spironolactone, GnRH modulators and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.[1] It is marketed in nearly every developed country except the US and Japan, where chlormadinone acetate is used instead.[1] It is prescription only, carries pregnancy category X, and is sold under brand names including Androcur, Cyprostat, Diane-35 and Dianette.[1] Beyond dermatology and hormone therapy it has been used for prostate cancer and, at high doses, to reduce sex drive in paraphilias, though it is now rarely used for prostate cancer.[1]

card.summary: Prescription antiandrogen used abroad for women's hair loss, acne and hirsutism, with liver, clot and meningioma risks.
card.note: Not marketed in the US; EMA warned in 2020 about meningioma at doses of 25 mg/day or more.

quick.overview:
Oral cyproterone acetate is a hormonal drug that blocks androgen receptors and acts as a progestin. In Europe and elsewhere it is prescribed to women for acne, excess hair growth and androgen-related scalp hair loss, often in a pill with ethinylestradiol.

It is not sold in the US and is generally considered impractical for men because of its hormonal effects.
quick.mechanism: It blocks androgen receptors, suppresses pituitary gonadotropins through its progestogenic action and so lowers androgen production, and is broken down mainly by the liver enzyme CYP3A4.
quick.risks: Documented risks include liver toxicity, venous blood clots, meningioma (EMA warning, 2020) and adrenal insufficiency on abrupt stop of high doses. Pregnancy, liver disease and prior clots are contraindications. It is prescription only.

angle.text: Prescribers use oral cyproterone acetate, alone or in a combined pill, to reduce acne, oiliness and excess hair and to slow androgenic hair thinning in women; in feminizing therapy it also suppresses testosterone.[1]
